lessonTitle: Isentropic Efficiency of Turbines, Pumps and Compressors

blocks.text: A turbine blade passage is polished and shaped to waste as little energy as possible, yet a real steam turbine still delivers only 80 to 90 percent of the work an ideal frictionless turbine would. Isentropic efficiency is the single number engineers use to say how close a machine comes.

blocks.markdown: In the ideal limit an adiabatic turbine, compressor or pump is reversible, so it is **isentropic**: entropy stays constant between inlet (1) and exit (2). The ideal exit state 2s lies at the exit pressure with the inlet entropy. Real machines have friction, leakage and turbulence, so the actual exit state 2a has greater entropy. Because the flow is adiabatic, the entropy can only increase.

blocks.title: Isentropic efficiency
blocks.text: Isentropic efficiency compares the actual device with the ideal isentropic device between the same inlet state and the same exit pressure. It is dimensionless and between 0 and 1 for any real adiabatic machine.

blocks.caption: Work output is the benefit, so actual over ideal; the ideal enthalpy drop is the largest possible
Work input is the cost, so ideal over actual; the ideal enthalpy rise is the smallest possible

blocks.title: Steam turbine with 85 % efficiency
blocks.prompt: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine with h1 = 3350 kJ/kg. At the exit pressure the isentropic exit enthalpy is h2s = 2250 kJ/kg (values supplied for the exercise). The isentropic efficiency is 0.85 and the mass flow rate is 20 kg/s. Find the actual exit enthalpy and the power.

steps.text: Actual specific work from the efficiency.
Actual exit enthalpy from the energy balance for an adiabatic turbine.

blocks.answer: h2a = 2415 kJ/kg, which is above the ideal value, and the power is 18.7 MW.

blocks.markdown: Why are the definitions inverted? Irreversibility makes a turbine produce **less** work than the ideal one and makes a compressor consume **more** work than the ideal one. If both were defined as actual divided by ideal, a compressor would have an efficiency above 1, which is meaningless. Putting the smaller quantity over the larger ensures $0<\eta\le1$ in both cases.

blocks.caption: In every case the actual exit state has a higher enthalpy than the isentropic one at the same exit pressure

blocks.title: Air compressor with 80 % efficiency
blocks.prompt: Air at 295 K is compressed adiabatically to a pressure ratio of 5. The isentropic efficiency is 0.80. Treat air as an ideal gas with cp = 1.005 kJ/(kg K) and k = 1.4. Find the actual work and the actual exit temperature.

steps.text: Actual work from the efficiency definition.
Actual exit temperature from the energy balance.

blocks.answer: w_a = 216.4 kJ/kg and T2a = 510 K, higher than the isentropic 467 K.

items: Find the inlet state and the exit pressure.
Find h2s (or T2s) from the isentropic process s2 = s1.
Apply the efficiency definition appropriate to the device.
Find h2a (or T2a) from the actual work and the energy balance.

blocks.title: Entropy rises in the real machine
blocks.text: The actual exit has higher entropy than the isentropic exit at the same pressure. On a T-s diagram the real path ends to the right of the vertical isentropic line.

blocks.title: Same pressure, not same state
blocks.text: Isentropic efficiency uses the same exit pressure for the real and ideal devices. It is not a comparison at the same exit temperature or the same exit entropy.

points: Isentropic efficiency compares a real adiabatic device with the isentropic one between the same inlet state and exit pressure.
For a turbine eta = (h1 - h2a)/(h1 - h2s), so h2a = h1 - eta (h1 - h2s).
For a compressor or pump eta = (h2s - h1)/(h2a - h1), so the actual work is the isentropic work divided by eta.
The definitions are inverted so that efficiency never exceeds 1: turbines give less than ideal, compressors need more.

questions.stem: Which expression gives the isentropic efficiency of an adiabatic compressor?

distractorRationale.d: Enthalpy ratios are not used, only differences.

questions.explanation: For a compressor the ideal work is the smallest possible, so efficiency is the ideal enthalpy rise over the actual enthalpy rise. The result is below 1 for a real machine.

questions.stem: An adiabatic steam turbine has an isentropic efficiency below 1. How does the actual exit enthalpy compare with the isentropic exit enthalpy at the same pressure?

options.text: It depends on mass flow rate

distractorRationale.b: A lower exit enthalpy would mean more work than the ideal.
distractorRationale.c: Equal only for an ideal turbine.
distractorRationale.d: Mass flow affects power, not specific enthalpies.

questions.explanation: The real turbine produces less work, so less energy leaves the steam and the exit enthalpy is higher than h2s. Friction and other irreversibilities add entropy at the exit.

questions.stem: A compressor delivers air to the same exit pressure. If its isentropic efficiency drops from 0.85 to 0.70, what happens to the actual specific work input?
questions.explanation: Since w_a = w_s/eta, a lower efficiency raises the actual work. The ratio of new to old work is 0.85/0.70 = 1.21, a 21 % increase.

questions.stem: Why is the isentropic efficiency of a compressor defined as ideal work divided by actual work, instead of actual over ideal?

options.text: So that the value is always below 1, since the real machine needs more work than the ideal one
Because compressors are more efficient than turbines
Because the ideal work is always larger for a compressor
Because enthalpy rises in a compressor and falls in a turbine

questions.correctOptionText: So that the value is always below 1, since the real machine needs more work than the ideal one

distractorRationale.b: The inversion is not related to relative merit.
distractorRationale.c: The ideal work is the smaller one.
distractorRationale.d: The direction of enthalpy change is not the reason.

questions.explanation: A real compressor needs more work than an isentropic one, so actual over ideal would exceed 1. The inverted definition keeps efficiency between 0 and 1 and so measures how close the real machine is to the ideal.

questions.stem: Steam expands adiabatically in a turbine of isentropic efficiency 0.9 to a pressure where the isentropic exit is wet steam. Compared with the isentropic exit state, the actual exit state has:

options.text: Lower entropy, lower enthalpy, wetter steam
Higher entropy, higher enthalpy, drier steam (higher quality)
The same entropy but higher enthalpy
Higher entropy, lower enthalpy, wetter steam

questions.correctOptionText: Higher entropy, higher enthalpy, drier steam (higher quality)

distractorRationale.a: Entropy cannot fall in an adiabatic process.
distractorRationale.d: Lower enthalpy would mean more work than the ideal.

questions.explanation: Irreversibility adds entropy and the real turbine extracts less work, so h2a exceeds h2s at the same pressure. At a given pressure in the wet region higher h and s correspond to a higher quality, so the real exit steam is drier.

questions.stem: A steam turbine has inlet enthalpy 3100 kJ/kg and isentropic exit enthalpy 2400 kJ/kg (values given). Its isentropic efficiency is 0.88. Find the actual exit enthalpy in kJ/kg.
questions.explanation: The ideal work is 700 kJ/kg and the actual work is 0.88 x 700 = 616 kJ/kg. The actual exit enthalpy is 3100 - 616 = 2484 kJ/kg.

questions.stem: Air at 290 K enters an adiabatic compressor and leaves at 8 times the inlet pressure. The isentropic efficiency is 0.82. Use cp = 1.005 kJ/(kg K) and k = 1.4. Find the actual specific work input in kJ/kg.
questions.explanation: The isentropic exit temperature is 290 x 8^0.2857 = 525.3 K, so w_s = 1.005 x (525.3 - 290) = 236.5 kJ/kg. Dividing by 0.82 gives w_a = 288.4 kJ/kg.

questions.stem: A pump raises liquid water (specific volume 0.001 m$^3$/kg, treated as incompressible) from 10 kPa to 5000 kPa. The isentropic efficiency of the pump is 0.70. Find the actual specific work input in kJ/kg.
questions.explanation: For an incompressible fluid the isentropic work is v (p2 - p1) = 0.001 x 4990 = 4.99 kJ/kg. The actual work is 4.99/0.70 = 7.13 kJ/kg, still small because liquids are nearly incompressible.

questions.stem: Explain why the isentropic efficiency of a turbine is defined as actual work over isentropic work, but that of a compressor is defined as isentropic work over actual work. Include what the actual exit state looks like on a T-s diagram.
markingGuide: Irreversibilities reduce the turbine output below the isentropic value
They increase the compressor input above the isentropic value
Inverting ensures efficiency lies between 0 and 1 for both
On a T-s diagram the actual exit lies to the right of the isentropic vertical line, with higher entropy (and higher enthalpy at the same pressure)
questions.explanation: Efficiency is the ratio of the lesser quantity of work to the greater, which reflects what the real machine achieves relative to the ideal. The actual path ends at higher entropy than the isentropic line because adiabatic irreversibility generates entropy.

questions.stem: A steam turbine receives 5 kg/s at h1 = 3000 kJ/kg and the isentropic exit enthalpy at the exit pressure is 2200 kJ/kg (values given). Its isentropic efficiency is 0.80. Find the power output and the actual exit enthalpy, and explain why the actual exit steam carries more energy than the isentropic exit steam.
markingGuide: Because less work is extracted, more energy remains in the steam, shown as a higher exit enthalpy caused by irreversibilities
questions.explanation: The actual work is 640 kJ/kg, giving 3200 kW, and the exit enthalpy is 2360 kJ/kg. The extra 160 kJ/kg left in the steam is the energy that irreversibilities failed to convert into shaft work.
